candidate.answerReason: Ten unordered pairs imply five council members. Choosing three of these five is equivalent to choosing the two left out, so there are also ten planning committees.

methods.label: Count pairs, then choose who stays out
methods.explanation:
First determine the number of council members. If there are \(n\) members, choosing a first person and then a different second person gives \(n(n-1)\) ordered selections. Each two-person team appears twice, once in each order. Thus
\[
\frac{n(n-1)}2=10,
\qquad n(n-1)=20.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\), this product increases as \(n\) increases. Since \(5\cdot4=20\), the council has exactly five members.

Now choosing a three-person planning committee is equivalent to choosing the two members left out. Each omitted pair determines exactly one committee, and each committee determines exactly one omitted pair. There are \(10\) such pairs. Serving on the welcoming committee does not remove anyone from consideration, because membership on both committees is allowed.

There are \(10\) planning committees, choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
methods.levelReason: The pair formula is derived by elementary counting, and the three-person count follows from a reversible complement correspondence. No factorial calculations are needed.
